margin.basis: Kaggle run 9: seven builds with the same cost within noise gave median p99 from 19.24 to 20.50 ms at 10240 bodies (6 percent) and 22.35 to 24.65 ms at 12288 (10 percent), and ticks over budget per three runs from 103 to 157 on a slow machine. Between machines the same build ran 11.7 ms (run 7), 13.6 ms (run 8) and 20.5 ms (run 9), so the gate compares with a reference build in the same run and not with a recorded absolute figure. Kaggle run 12, the same source as reference and candidate: p99 13.5 to 14.3 ms and 13.7 to 14.5 ms over five runs each, zero ticks over budget, except one candidate run at 19.5 ms with 17 ticks over. So both figures are judged on the median run, with 10 percent on the p99 and 25 percent plus 2 ticks on the count. With the awake budget the top tier runs near 6 ms, where 10 percent is 0.6 ms: Kaggle runs 21 and 22, the same source as reference and candidate, gave medians of 6.83 against 6.26 ms and 5.83 against 6.16 ms, with single repeats from 5.56 to 9.84 ms. So the p99 limit is the larger of the reference times 1.10 and the reference plus 1 ms. At 40960 bodies nearly every tick of the run has bodies awake, and the p99 moves with the host: Kaggle runs 27 and 28, the same source as reference and candidate, gave p99 medians of 7.96 against 9.30 ms over every tick (run 27, which failed the 1.10 rule) and 9.08 against 8.05 ms over quiet ticks (run 28). The mean tick while bodies are awake is steady: 5.39 against 5.57 ms, 5.97 against 5.86 ms, and 5.40 against 5.54 and 5.06 against 5.12 ms in runs 24 and 25, within 3 percent. So the build is compared on that mean with a 10 percent margin, and the p99 over quiet ticks is a tail guard at 25 percent or 1 ms.

marble.basis: Kaggle runs 8 and 9: every tick over 16.7 ms in a first run falls at the first impact (ticks 75 to 83) on cold code; later runs peak at 12 to 20.3 ms of CPU time with zero runqueue wait, and p99 stays at or under 15.0 ms. Kaggle run 21, on the Xeon class: one tick of 29.0 ms (tick 202 of one run of four on the 64 MiB tier, CPU time equal to wall time, no runqueue wait) while the other three runs of the same deterministic scenario peaked at 13.5 to 14.8 ms. The bench shows the same single stalls on that class (19.8 and 41.9 ms between ticks of 6 ms with the same awake count). A stall that is not repeated at the same tick is the host, so a tick over 25 ms counts when it is over in at least half of the timed runs at the same tick index; single ones stay in the verdict as over25InAnyRun.

drift.basis: The reference build is a fixed source, so only the machine, Node and the bench harness can move its figure. Kaggle runs 16 to 19 all landed on class GenuineIntel-6-79-0: the same build at the same count ran a median p99 of 13.5 ms in run 16 and 8.8 to 9.0 ms in runs 17 to 19, 1.5 times apart, while the single-thread calibration differed by 1.10 (636 against 575 ms). So one class spreads by about 1.4 times beyond what the calibration explains, and the limit is the recorded reference p99 times 1.5, times the ratio of the calibration of the run to the recorded one when the machine calibrates slower. A drift under that is not caught. At the 40960 tier the drift is judged on the reference mean tick while bodies are awake, not its p99: on class GenuineIntel-6-79-0 that mean ran 4.17 ms in run 32, 5.39 ms in run 27 and 5.97 ms in run 28, 1.43 times apart with calibrations 1.10 apart, where its quiet-tick p99 ran 5.05 to 9.08 ms.
